o: Sum digit * (number of occurrences of that digit) over the decimal representation of n. For 122 that is 1*1 + 2*2 = 5; for 101 it is 0*1 + 1*2 = 2. With n up to 1e9 (10 digits), any straightforward digit-counting method works instantly.
k: Zero contributes nothing to the score even when present.
Both string conversion and repeated division extract the digits in O(log n).

a.i: Convert n to its decimal string and tally character frequencies; multiply each digit by its count and add up.
s: Count occurrences of each digit character.
Return the sum of digit-value times count.
a.t: O(log n) — proportional to the number of digits

a.i: Repeatedly take n % 10 and divide by 10, accumulating digit * 1 per occurrence directly — equivalent to summing the digits of n, since each occurrence contributes its own value once.
s: While n > 0: add n % 10 to the score and set n //= 10.
a.t: O(log n) — one iteration per digit

w: A neat realization worth mentioning in interviews: the score equals the plain digit sum of n, since freq-weighting each distinct digit reproduces the sum of all digits. Either approach is instant at these constraints. Watch for the n = 0 edge if constraints ever change (loop-based version returns 0, which is correct). Follow-up: score of n^2, or score in another base.
